development-methods-s2.title: Shy toddlers, shy teens?
development-methods-s2.html:
Introduction

Some toddlers freeze and go quiet around strangers; others walk right up to them. Researchers asked whether this early shyness lasts into the teen years.

Participants

120 children from one Midwestern city, recruited at age 2 through pediatric clinics (52% girls; 70% White, 18% Black, 12% Latino). 96 were still in the study at age 15. Parents gave informed consent, children gave their own assent at ages 7 and 15, and a university IRB approved the study. Names were replaced by code numbers.

Method

At age 2, observers watching through a one-way window rated how long each child took to approach a friendly stranger. At 7 and again at 15, each child spent 10 minutes in a waiting room with an unfamiliar peer, and coders counted how many times the child spoke first. No conditions were assigned.

Results

Toddlers who were slowest to approach the stranger tended to speak first fewer times at 15 (r=−.45r = -.45). Even so, about half of the shyest toddlers were in the typical range by 15.

Discussion

Early shyness predicted teen shyness to a moderate degree, but many shy toddlers changed.

Invented study for practice.

physical-development-s1.title: The visual cliff
physical-development-s1.html:
Introduction

Eleanor Gibson and Richard Walk asked whether babies who have just learned to crawl can perceive depth, and whether they avoid a drop.

Participants

36 infants aged 6 to 14 months, each tested with their mother. Young animals of several species were also tested.

Method

Each baby was placed on a board in the middle of a glass table. Under the glass on one side, a checkered pattern sat right below (the shallow side); on the other side, the same pattern lay far below (the deep side, the "cliff"). The glass made both sides safe. The mother called the baby from one side and then the other, and researchers recorded which way each baby crawled.

Results

Of the 27 babies who moved off the center board, all crawled onto the shallow side at least once. Only 3 crept onto the deep side. Many babies called from the deep side crawled away from their mother or cried.

Discussion

Most crawling babies perceive depth. Later research found that wariness of the drop grows with crawling experience, so experience and maturation both play a part.

physical-development-s3.title: Smoking during pregnancy and birth weight
physical-development-s3.html:
Introduction

Researchers asked whether smoking during pregnancy is linked to lower birth weight.

Participants

400 pregnant women at two city hospitals, who gave informed consent. Their records were kept confidential under code numbers.

Method

At the first prenatal visit, each woman reported how many cigarettes she smoked per day. Nurses weighed each baby at birth. The researchers did not ask anyone to smoke or to stop; they compared the groups as they were.

Results

Babies of women who smoked 10 or more cigarettes a day weighed on average 250 grams less than babies of nonsmokers. Babies of light smokers fell in between.

Invented study for practice.

gender-orientation-s1.title: Four questions about a person

gender-orientation-s2.title: Toy labels and preschoolers’ play
gender-orientation-s2.html:
Introduction

Researchers asked whether telling children that a new toy is "for girls" or "for boys" changes how long they play with it.

Participants

80 children aged 4 and 5 (40 girls, 40 boys) at four preschools in one city. Parents gave informed consent, each child agreed to play, and any child could stop at any time.

Method

Each child was randomly assigned to one of two conditions. A researcher showed the child an unfamiliar toy (a set of colored gears) and said either "This is a toy for girls" or "This is a toy for boys." The child then had 20 minutes of free play in a room with the gears and other toys. A coder who did not know the condition recorded how many minutes the child played with the gears.

Results

When the gears were labeled for their own gender, children played with them for a mean of 13 minutes; when labeled for the other gender, a mean of 6 minutes. The difference was statistically significant and was similar for girls and boys.

Discussion

A single label changed play, suggesting that children use gender labels to decide what is "for me."

Invented study for practice.

cognitive-development-s1.title: Conservation of liquid at ages 4, 6 and 8
cognitive-development-s1.html:
Introduction

Researchers asked at what age children understand that pouring water into a differently shaped glass does not change how much water there is.

Participants

90 children from three public elementary schools in one city: 30 aged 4, 30 aged 6 and 30 aged 8 (about half girls). Parents gave informed consent, each child agreed to play "a water game," and children could stop at any time. Results were reported only as group totals.

Method

Each child saw two identical short glasses with the same amount of water and agreed they held the same amount. While the child watched, the researcher poured one glass into a tall, thin glass and asked, "Is there more water in this glass, more in that glass, or the same in both?" A child passed the task by saying "the same" and giving a reason, such as "You only poured it." Each child was tested once.

Results

The percentage of children who passed rose with age: 10% at age 4, 40% at 6 and 87% at 8. Most children who failed said the tall glass had more water.

Discussion

Understanding of conservation grew sharply between 4 and 8, but there was wide variation within each age group.

Invented study for practice.

language-development-s1.title: Milestones of early speech

language-development-s2.title: Babies hearing sounds from other languages
language-development-s2.html:
Introduction

Janet Werker and Richard Tees asked whether babies raised hearing English can tell apart speech sounds that English does not use but Hindi and a First Nations language (Nthlakampx) do.

Participants

Infants from English-speaking homes in Canada, tested at 6 to 8, 8 to 10 and 10 to 12 months, some of them followed across these ages. Infants learning Hindi or Nthlakampx were also tested.

Method

Each baby heard one speech sound repeated, then a switch to a similar sound. Babies were trained to turn their heads toward a toy display when they heard the sound change; a head turn right after a switch counted as noticing the difference.

Results

Most 6- to 8-month-olds from English-speaking homes noticed the non-English sound differences. By 10 to 12 months, few did. Babies learning Hindi or Nthlakampx still noticed the differences in their own languages at 10 to 12 months.

Discussion

Babies start able to hear sound differences from many languages and, by their first birthday, tune in to the sounds of the language around them.

social-emotional-development-s1.title: Cloth and wire mothers
social-emotional-development-s1.html:
Introduction

In the 1950s, many psychologists believed infants bond with their mothers mainly because mothers feed them. Harry Harlow tested this idea with infant rhesus monkeys.

Participants

Infant rhesus monkeys separated from their mothers shortly after birth and raised in a laboratory.

Method

Each infant’s cage held two artificial "mothers": one made of bare wire and one covered in soft terry cloth. For some infants, only the wire mother held a milk bottle; for others, only the cloth mother did. Researchers recorded how much time each infant spent on each mother and where it ran when frightened by a noisy mechanical toy.

Results

Infants spent most of each day clinging to the cloth mother, even when only the wire mother gave milk; they went to the wire mother only to feed. When frightened, they ran to the cloth mother and, after clinging to it, began to explore.

Discussion

Comfort from soft touch, not feeding alone, drove the bond. Monkeys raised with no real mother later showed lasting problems with social behavior and parenting. These studies caused serious, lasting harm to the animals and are widely criticized today; current animal-care rules would not allow them.

classical-conditioning-s1.title: Invented study: a tone, a puff of air and an eye blink
classical-conditioning-s1.html:
Introduction

Researchers asked whether a tone that is followed by a puff of air to the eye can come to cause an eye blink on its own.

Participants

24 college students (ages 18 to 23; 14 women and 10 men) volunteered. Each gave informed consent and could stop at any time. The puff was gentle and harmless.

Method

On each trial a tone sounded for half a second and was followed at once by a light puff of air to one eye, which makes people blink without learning. After 40 pairings, the tone was played alone 20 times (no puff). The next day the tone was played alone 5 more times. A sensor recorded a blink as any eyelid closure within half a second after the tone began.

Results

Before any pairing, students blinked to the tone on 5% of trials. After 40 pairings they blinked to the tone alone on 80% of trials. By the end of the 20 tone-alone trials this fell to 10%. On the first tone of the next day it rose to 45%.

Invented study for practice.

operant-conditioning-s1.title: Invented data: cumulative lever presses on four schedules

operant-conditioning-s2.title: Invented study: rewards on every try or some tries
operant-conditioning-s2.html:
Introduction

Researchers asked whether being rewarded every time or only some of the time changes how long people keep trying once rewards stop.

Participants

40 high school students (ages 15 to 18) from two schools in Ohio took part with a parent's permission and their own assent. They were randomly assigned to two groups of 20.

Method

Students played a simple online game, pressing a button to try to win points. In the every-time group, every press won a point for the first 60 presses. In the some-times group, presses won a point at random, on average every fourth press. Then, without warning, presses stopped winning points in both groups. Persistence was the number of presses each student made before choosing to quit, up to a limit of 200. Students were debriefed at the end.

Results

After points stopped, the every-time group made a mean of 24 presses before quitting. The some-times group made a mean of 71 presses.

Invented study for practice.

social-cognitive-learning-s1.title: Invented data: rats in a maze, with and without food

social-cognitive-learning-s2.title: Invented study: copying a model who builds a tower
social-cognitive-learning-s2.html:
Introduction

Researchers asked whether children copy a new behavior more often when they see the model rewarded for it.

Participants

60 children aged 4 and 5 from three preschools took part with written consent from a parent. Each child also agreed to play and could stop at any time. Children were randomly assigned to one of three groups of 20.

Method

Each child watched a two-minute video of an adult building a tower in an unusual way: blocks stacked in a zigzag, then tapped twice with a spoon. In the model-rewarded group, the adult got praise and a prize at the end. In the model-scolded group, the adult was told "That is not how we play." In the no-consequence group, the video simply ended. Each child was then left alone with the blocks and spoon for five minutes, and a coder who did not know the child's group counted how many of the model's six actions the child copied.

Results

Children copied a mean of 4.1 actions in the model-rewarded group, 2.6 in the no-consequence group and 1.2 in the model-scolded group.

Invented study for practice.

The observer is rewarded for the exact behavior
The model is punished in front of the observer
The observer is shaped through successive approximations

items.q: On day 10 the "food from day 9" group suddenly makes about as few errors as the group fed every day. What does this show?
options: They had learned the maze earlier without showing it
One day of food taught them the whole maze
Rats that get no food at the goal learn nothing about a maze
The rats had habituated to the maze

items.q: Which concept names what the day-9 rats most likely formed during days 1 to 8?
options: A cognitive map
A conditioned taste aversion
A secondary reinforcer
An unconditioned response

items.q: Find the mean number of wrong turns for the "never fed" group across days 1 to 4.

mistakes.why: 38 is the total for the four days. Divide by 4.
7.75 is the mean of the "food every day" group. Use the never-fed line.

items.q: What is the independent variable in this study?
options: The consequence the model received in the video
The number of the model's actions each child copied
The children's age
The coder's knowledge of each child's group

items.q: Which concept best explains why children in the model-scolded group copied the fewest actions?
options: Vicarious punishment
Negative reinforcement
Latent learning
Insight learning

items.q: Why did the researchers use a coder who did not know which group each child was in?
options: To keep expectations from biasing the counts
To make sure the sample represented preschoolers in general
To give the children informed consent
To randomly assign children to groups

items.q: Write the operational definition of imitation used in this study.

specific.model: Imitation was measured as the number of the model's six actions a child copied, counted by a coder, during five minutes alone with the blocks and spoon.

opdef.label: What was counted
options: the number of the model's six actions a child copied
how much a child liked the model
whether a child watched the whole video

why.1: Liking the model was not measured.
why.2: Watching the video was part of the procedure, not the measure.

when.label: When
options: five minutes alone with the blocks and spoon
the two-minute video

why.1: The video came first; copying was counted afterward, during the five minutes of play.
